name: Homo floresiensis ("the Hobbit")
hook: A 1-metre skeleton in a Flores cave, dismissed as a sick modern human, is now a distinct hominin species.
claim: Skeletal remains from Liang Bua cave on Flores belong to a new, very small-bodied and small-brained hominin species, Homo floresiensis, that made stone tools and survived far later than any other archaic hominin known in Asia.

claimed_age.label: Present from before ~38,000 to at least ~18,000 years ago
claimed_age.basis: Radiocarbon, luminescence, uranium-series and ESR dating of the Liang Bua sequence (Morwood et al. 2004); the wider H. floresiensis-bearing deposits were bracketed at about 95,000-12,000 years.

accepted_age.label: ~100,000-60,000 years (skeleton); tools to ~50,000 years
accepted_age.basis: 2016 redating (TL, IRSL/pIRIR, 40Ar/39Ar, radiocarbon) in a sequence spanning ~190,000 years to the present; stone tools linked to the taxon continue to ~50,000 years ago.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: Late Pleistocene Island Southeast Asia was assumed occupied only by modern Homo sapiens; no other hominin was expected to survive there almost to the present.

unambiguous_signal.note: The bones are unambiguously a small-bodied hominin skeleton; whether they represent a new species rather than a pathological modern human was disputed from the outset.

documented_context.note: LB1 and later individuals were excavated in situ over controlled seasons by the joint Indonesian-Australian team under an official research permit.

multiple_dating_methods.note: The original 2004 chronology combined radiocarbon, luminescence, uranium-series and ESR dating of the same sequence.

multiple_labs.note: Co-author affiliations include University of New England (Morwood) and University of Wollongong (Roberts, a luminescence specialist), among others.

professional_recovery.note: Excavated by the joint Indonesian Centre for Archaeology / University of New England team under Indonesian government permit (2003 season).

peer_reviewed_report.note: Two companion papers in Nature, October 2004, describing the skeleton and its archaeological and dating context.

material_accessible.note: For about three months in 2005 the type specimen was held and studied by a rival Indonesian researcher rather than the describing team, before being returned.

independent_teams.note: Within five years, groups distinct from the excavators (Jacob et al. 2006; Hershkovitz et al. 2007) published independent pathology-based reinterpretations.

proponent_stake.note: An academic Indonesian-Australian excavation project; no commercial, religious or nationalist motive documented for the describing team.

objections.text: LB1 is not a new species but comes from a small-bodied ('pygmy') Australomelanesian modern human population; LB1 itself also shows microcephaly and other developmental abnormalities.
objections.outcome_note: LB1's virtual endocast is not microcephalic or pygmy in shape (Falk et al. 2005); 2013 geometric morphometrics grouped LB1 with archaic Homo, not modern humans (Baab et al. 2013).

objections.text: The small stature and small head are explained by Laron syndrome, a growth-hormone-insensitivity disorder documented in modern human populations of the region.
objections.raised_by: Israel Hershkovitz, Liora Kornreich, Zvi Laron
objections.outcome_note: A 2013 geometric-morphometric comparison found LB1's cranial shape clearly distinct from Laron-syndrome and healthy modern humans alike, grouping instead with fossil Homo, closest to H. erectus.

objections.text: LB1's brain size and limb proportions match Down syndrome in a small-bodied modern human population, not diagnostic traits of a new species.
objections.raised_by: Maciej Henneberg, Robert B. Eckhardt and colleagues
objections.outcome_note: A 2016 re-evaluation, co-authored by original describer Peter Brown and endocast specialist Dean Falk, compared LB1 to clinical Down-syndrome samples and found it does not match the Down-syndrome pattern.

objections.text: It is unclear whether H. floresiensis is a dwarfed descendant of Asian Homo erectus or instead descends from an earlier, already small-brained hominin lineage that left Africa before H. erectus.
objections.raised_by: Framed as an open question by van den Bergh et al. 2016
objections.outcome_note: Mata Menge fossils (700 ka) are as small as Liang Bua H. floresiensis and closest to early Asian H. erectus, favouring dwarfing from H. erectus; deep phylogeny still debated.

status_note: The new-species view is now accepted, supported by primitive wrist and brain anatomy, at least nine individuals, and ~700,000-year-old small-bodied ancestors at Mata Menge. A small minority still argue for pathology.
what_settled_it: Comparative-morphology studies (2005-2016) repeatedly distinguished the Flores skeletons from microcephalic, Laron-syndrome and Down-syndrome humans, grouping them with archaic Homo; ~700,000-year-old Mata Menge fossils showed the lineage was ancient, not one pathological individual.

timeline.event: A joint Indonesian-Australian team excavates the LB1 skeleton at Liang Bua cave, Flores.
Brown et al. and Morwood et al. name Homo floresiensis in Nature, dating LB1 to ~18,000 years within a ~95,000-12,000 year sequence.
Teuku Jacob takes the type specimen to his own laboratory for about three months, restricting the describing team's access.
Falk et al. publish a virtual endocast study finding LB1's brain shape is not microcephalic or pygmy.
Jacob et al. argue in PNAS that the remains are a small-bodied modern human population, with LB1 individually microcephalic.
Tocheri et al. report LB1's wrist bones retain a primitive, pre-modern-human form.
Hershkovitz et al. propose LB1 represents Laron syndrome in a local inbred population.
Henneberg, Eckhardt and colleagues argue in PNAS that LB1 shows the skeletal signature of Down syndrome.
Sutikna et al. revise the Liang Bua chronology: skeletal remains ~100,000-60,000 years old, stone tools to ~50,000 years.
Baab, Brown, Falk and Richtsmeier publish a critical evaluation rejecting the Down-syndrome diagnosis for LB1.
Van den Bergh et al. report ~700,000-year-old small-bodied hominin fossils at Mata Menge, resembling early Asian H. erectus.
Kaifu et al. describe an even smaller humerus and teeth from Mata Menge, confirming a diminutive lineage since at least ~700,000 years ago.

decisive_tests.test: Attempt ancient-DNA or palaeoproteomic extraction from Liang Bua or Mata Menge skeletal material using current tropical-preservation protocols.
decisive_tests.would_show: Direct genetic or protein-based placement of H. floresiensis relative to H. erectus and other hominins, and whether it falls within modern human variation.

decisive_tests.test: Compare LB1's skeleton and endocast to enlarged clinical reference samples of Down syndrome and Laron syndrome using the same geometric-morphometric protocol used in 2013-2016.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the pathology diagnoses hold up against a larger comparative clinical sample than previously available.

falsifier: Ancient DNA or proteomics placing the Liang Bua skeletons within normal Homo sapiens variation, or a larger clinical comparison showing LB1 falls within the Down-syndrome or Laron-syndrome range rather than with archaic Homo, would overturn the new-species interpretation.

sources.citation: Brown, P., Sutikna, T., Morwood, M.J., Soejono, R.P. et al. (2004). A new small-bodied hominin from the Late Pleistocene of Flores, Indonesia. Nature 431(7012): 1055-1061.
sources.note: Crossref metadata confirmed; no OpenAlex abstract, full text paywalled. LB1's description is corroborated by later checked sources (S3, S11) that cite and recap its findings.

sources.citation: Morwood, M.J., Soejono, R.P., Roberts, R.G., Sutikna, T. et al. (2004). Archaeology and age of a new hominin from Flores in eastern Indonesia. Nature 431(7012): 1087-1091.
sources.note: Abstract read via page fetch: 4 dating methods (14C, luminescence, U-series, ESR); species dated before ~38 to at least ~18 kyr; H. erectus-origin hypothesis; multi-institution author list.

sources.citation: Falk, D., Hildebolt, C., Smith, K., Morwood, M.J. et al. (2005). The Brain of LB1, Homo floresiensis. Science 308(5719): 242-245.
sources.note: Full abstract read: LB1 is not a microcephalic or pygmy; brain/body ratio scales like an australopithecine but endocast shape resembles H. erectus.

sources.citation: Culotta, E. (2005). Battle Erupts Over the 'Hobbit' Bones. Science 307(5713): 1179.
sources.note: Teaser text read: for three months a rival researcher held the skeleton, invited other researchers to examine it, and removed a rib sample for DNA analysis.

sources.citation: Jacob, T., Indriati, E., Soejono, R.P., Hsu, K. et al. (2006). Pygmoid Australomelanesian Homo sapiens skeletal remains from Liang Bua, Flores: Population affinities and pathological abnormalities. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 103(36): 13421-13426.
sources.note: Full abstract read: proposes LB1 from an earlier pygmy H. sapiens population with individual microcephaly; other remains share small body size but not microcephaly.

sources.citation: Argue, D., Donlon, D., Groves, C., Wright, R. (2006). Homo floresiensis: Microcephalic, pygmoid, Australopithecus, or Homo?. Journal of Human Evolution 51(4): 360-374.
sources.note: Crossref metadata confirmed; publisher page returned no readable text (paywalled). Widely cited as an early rebuttal of the pygmy/microcephaly hypotheses; not used alone to support a key field.

sources.citation: Tocheri, M.W., Orr, C.M., Larson, S.G., Sutikna, T. et al. (2007). The Primitive Wrist of Homo floresiensis and Its Implications for Hominin Evolution. Science 317(5845): 1743-1745.
sources.note: Full abstract read: LB1 wrist bones retain morphology primitive for the African ape-human clade, unlike derived Neandertal/modern-human wrists; argues against an undiagnosed-pathology explanation.

sources.citation: Hershkovitz, I., Kornreich, L., Laron, Z. (2007). Comparative skeletal features between Homo floresiensis and patients with primary growth hormone insensitivity (Laron syndrome). American Journal of Physical Anthropology 134(2): 198-208.
sources.note: Full abstract read: proposes the Flores remains are a local, highly inbred H. sapiens population with a growth-hormone-receptor mutation (Laron syndrome), not a new species.

sources.citation: Baab, K.L., McNulty, K.P., Harvati, K. (2013). Homo floresiensis Contextualized: A Geometric Morphometric Comparative Analysis of Fossil and Pathological Human Samples. PLoS ONE 8(7): e69119.
sources.note: Full abstract read: geometric morphometrics show LB1 distinct from healthy, hypothyroid and Laron-syndrome modern humans; LB1 groups with archaic Homo, closest to H. erectus.

sources.citation: Henneberg, M., Eckhardt, R.B., Chavanaves, S., Hsu, K.J. (2014). Evolved developmental homeostasis disturbed in LB1 from Flores, Indonesia, denotes Down syndrome and not diagnostic traits of the invalid species Homo floresiensis. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 111(33): 11967-11972.
sources.note: Full abstract read: LB1's endocranial volume and femur/foot proportions argued to fall in the range predicted for Down syndrome in a normal small-bodied regional population.

sources.citation: Sutikna, T., Tocheri, M.W., Morwood, M.J., Saptomo, E.W. et al. (2016). Revised stratigraphy and chronology for Homo floresiensis at Liang Bua in Indonesia. Nature 532(7599): 366-369.
sources.note: Abstract and Nature editor summary read via page fetch: skeleton-bearing strata older than first thought; the previous ~18 kyr age for LB1 and ~95-12 kyr deposit range are not supported.

sources.citation: Baab, K.L., Brown, P., Falk, D., Richtsmeier, J.T. et al. (2016). A Critical Evaluation of the Down Syndrome Diagnosis for LB1, Type Specimen of Homo floresiensis. PLOS ONE 11(6): e0155731.
sources.note: Full abstract read: re-evaluated Down-syndrome features against clinical Down-syndrome and euploid samples via morphometrics; co-authored by describer P. Brown and endocast expert D. Falk.

sources.citation: van den Bergh, G.D., Kaifu, Y., Kurniawan, I., Kono, R.T. et al. (2016). Homo floresiensis-like fossils from the early Middle Pleistocene of Flores. Nature 534(7606): 245-248.
sources.note: Nature editor summary read via page fetch: Mata Menge mandible/teeth, as small as or smaller than Liang Bua H. floresiensis, dated ~700,000 years; morphology supports derivation from Asian H. erectus.

sources.citation: Sutikna, T., Tocheri, M.W., Faith, J.T., Jatmiko et al. (2018). The spatio-temporal distribution of archaeological and faunal finds at Liang Bua (Flores, Indonesia) in light of the revised chronology for Homo floresiensis. Journal of Human Evolution 124: 52-74.
sources.note: Full abstract read: skeletal remains ~100-60 ka; cultural (stone-tool) evidence to ~50 ka; H. floresiensis, Stegodon, marabou stork and vulture likely extinct by ~50 ka; sequence spans ~190 ka.

sources.citation: Kaifu, Y., Kurniawan, I., Mizushima, S., Sawada, J. et al. (2024). Early evolution of small body size in Homo floresiensis. Nature Communications 15(1).
sources.note: Full abstract read: Mata Menge adult humerus 9-16% shorter/thinner than the Liang Bua type specimen; diminutive body size on Flores since at least ~700,000 years, likely from early Asian H. erectus.

confidence_note: Nearly every objection and rebuttal is grounded in a directly read abstract or excerpt. The gap is Brown et al. (2004), confirmed via Crossref metadata and content described in later checked sources.
corrections: Starter notes give the original age simply as '~18,000 years'. Morwood et al. (2004) claimed H. floresiensis existed from before ~38,000 to at least ~18,000 years ago, within deposits bracketed at ~95,000-12,000 years.

The 2016 revision is not one number: Sutikna et al. (2016, 2018) date the skeletal remains to ~100,000-60,000 years, while stone-tool evidence for the taxon persists to ~50,000 years, in a sequence spanning ~190,000 years.

Starter notes list three pathology hypotheses as if concurrent; they were proposed in sequence by separate groups (Jacob et al. 2006; Hershkovitz et al. 2007; Henneberg/Eckhardt et al. 2014), each later addressed by its own rebuttal study.
notes: No ancient DNA or protein sequence from H. floresiensis is published as of 2026; a rib taken during the 2005 custody dispute does not appear to have yielded reported results. 'Hobbit' is a press nickname, not a formal designation. At least nine individuals are now attributed to the species, one reason a single-individual pathology reading is now a minority view. Mundane checks: excavation was by a credentialed team under permit; stratigraphic complexity, not fraud, explains the original age mismatch. Henneberg and Eckhardt's group still defends the Down-syndrome reading; this record treats that as unresolved dissent, not disproof of the rebuttal.

plates.caption: A reconstructed Homo floresiensis skull cast, showing the small braincase central to the microcephaly debate.
